title: High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia?
text: High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia? Expert comment jon.wallace 25 November 2026 An unpopular government must train its civil service how to deliver a strategy at a time of technological upheaval – while persuading a sceptical public. It has some resources to draw on. The significant increase in German defence spending since 2022 has been celebrated as a success story for European security. Germany has the stated ambition to become the largest land power in Europe, with a core defence budget set to rise to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2029. To support this effort, some initial procurement reforms are already taking place: plans were unveiled earlier in the year to reform the defence procurement agency. But Germany still struggles with the strategic and cultural transformation across society that will be necessary to realize its ambitions. In its political and military leadership, there is an incomplete understanding of how German deterrence is meant to work, what kind of a future conflict to expect and as a result, what systems Germany needs to acquire. That risks making the increased defence spending inefficient, undermining fragile public support for rearmament. And it could send confusing signals to industry. The challenge is complex. And it comes at a time of technological, political and strategic upheaval. But Germany has important resources to draw on. A clear strategy Like many NATO allies, Germany has updated its security and defence strategic documents over the last few years. At first glance, these look comparable to those of other NATO nations. But Germany continues to struggle to translate them into action. Part of this challenge might be that some documents, such as the Bundeswehr’s military strategy published in 2026, were produced for the first time. Other NATO countries have established pathways for turning a strategy into action, but Germany has to figure it out from scratch. What’s more, in some cases procurement has come ahead of the strategy. That partly makes sense: Germany could not wait until 2026 to start acquiring new systems, considering the changed security environment. But it also seems to have inhibited procurement reform, sent mixed messages to industry and led to some disjointed and traditional contracts.  Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape? Examples of this include post-contract adjustments to a large order of Boxer armoured vehicles. Additionally, traditional procurement types have been prioritized to date: orders placed have tended towards big, traditional equipment – frigates, helicopters, armoured vehicles. These are all important and the Bundeswehr needs more of them. However, in the NATO comparison, the Bundeswehr compares poorly for orders placed for uncrewed systems and digital support infrastructure. Meanwhile, Berlin is struggling to adapt to the pace of technological change in war, and its effect on deterrence. Newer military technologies complicate old assumptions about the balance between conventional and nuclear deterrence. Some advanced conventional capabilities, such as deep precision strike, are taking on parts of a traditionally nuclear deterrence mission. But NATO thinking since the end of the cold war created silos where nuclear and conventional capabilities were seen as entirely separate, rather than as levers of the same concept of deterrence. This means that non-nuclear allies like Germany have not invested much thought in how their militaries can deter. Conventional militaries’ role was traditionally to defend, not deter aggression or fight to win. The absence of good understanding of what to deter and what kind of fight to expect hampers German decision making when it comes to military procurement. Germany now needs to find a way to upskill its officials and civil servants to better understand deterrence concepts, especially how to tailor deterrence according to the perceptions of its potential adversaries. These discussions must be had across a broad spectrum of the German political and military leadership. There needs to be a consensus understanding of what Russia has learned from the war in Ukraine, how it is applying these lessons to its thinking about war with NATO, and what capability gaps Germany and other NATO countries have. Public opinion Germany’s security leadership also faces a domestic challenge. The German government has struggled to take the public along with its messaging on the re-armament agenda and especially support for Ukraine. Chancellor Friedrich Merz won election on a platform that included stronger support for Ukraine. But his handling of domestic issues has seen his popularity plunge to the lowest on record for a German chancellor . Falling support for the government is mirrored by the rise of the far-right party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). A significant majority of its supporters oppose support for Ukraine, and its leadership does not see Russia as a threat to Germany . It would likely be a serious challenge to EU and NATO cooperation on European security were the AfD to become a party of government. Mending fences An additional political factor Germany has to navigate is how to define its new European security leadership role in relation to its neighbours. Allies like Poland remain uncomfortable with the idea of Germany providing security leadership for Europe. That is especially true in the context of rising AfD support. ‘We remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,’ said Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski in September, following the AfD’s record result in the regional Saxony-Anhalt election.  Germany and Poland will both be part of the negotiations for upcoming Ukraine peace talks. Polish negotiators will undoubtedly watch very carefully for any signs of German concessions towards Russia, as Poland has long been critical of the former German approach of prioritizing business relations with Russia. These factors combine for a difficult burden: Germany needs to navigate internal cultural and structural reform as well as a difficult domestic landscape, while being under the scrutiny of its allies. The way forward Germany does have resources it can draw on. When seeking to upskill its officials in deterrence doctrine, it can learn from NATO partners’ plans: the UK also recognized it has lost deterrence knowledge across its civil service and is running regular training courses for civil servants. Germany also has a vibrant academic community specializing in strategic thinking – people who would welcome working more closely with government and delivering some of this work. Polish concerns about Russia and its suspicion of Germany run deep. Procurement reform has been written about widely, but a simple and affordable improvement might be for the German government to be more disciplined in publishing a list of priorities for procurement , so that industry can react and compete accordingly. Perhaps more challenging is how to better engage Germany’s neighbours. The German government has tried a range of different confidence-building measures with Poland, similar to its efforts that helped transform the relationship with France.  However, Polish concerns about Russia and its suspicion of Germany run deep. It will take time to strengthen those relationships. Germany will also have to demonstrate that the ‘ Zeitenwende ’ is a real, long-term, sustained change, maintaining its current focus on security and defence. Its leading role in the NATO forward deployment, and participation in joint Baltic and Eastern flank exercises will play a significant role here. In order to bring its people along, the German government needs to develop a sustained and coherent narrative about the risk the country faces from Russia, and all that it is doing to keep Germany safe, and German democracy strong and free.  It will also need to improve its messaging especially for young Germans. It must highlight the opportunities it is creating for them, rather than scaring them with mixed messages on forced conscription – when they are already dissatisfied with their employment and educational opportunities.
